we are updating the dye log for the north room at alder mill for the week beginning april eighth and this is the second copy because the first copy got damp beside the sampling sink the log covers the indigo vat the madder kettle and the small walnut drum and it should let the next shift follow what happened without relying on anyone's memory each entry has a time a vessel name an operator and the shade card number the cards stay in the gray binder on the shelf above the scale and not in the sample drawer because that drawer is kept for wet swatches the room was cool on monday morning at eighteen degrees and the west window was open for twenty minutes while the exhaust fan was inspected
new paragraph on monday the indigo vat was charged at seven ten with thirty two liters of softened water and the night shift had already weighed six hundred grams of natural indigo and one point two kilograms of salt into separate covered tubs the salt went in first and the dye powder was sifted slowly after the water circulated for four minutes the pH strip read ten point eight and the technician wrote that the surface looked coppery rather than blue there were two foam islands near the paddle but no dry powder at the edge the first blue cotton test was shade card I twelve and the second was I thirteen so both pieces were tied to the same card ring until they could be checked in daylight at the north table
new paragraph tuesday's madder kettle held eighteen kilos of wool yarn in four tied skeins the water reached eighty two degrees at nine twenty and stayed below a simmer while the crew stirred with the long maple stick the alum measure was four hundred and fifty grams not five hundred because the supplier's bag had arrived short and the remaining amount was reserved for the small trial pot the first skein came out pinker than the other three so it went back for six minutes with the basket turned once at the three minute mark the log includes a note that the shade can shift as the wool dries and the supervisor asked for a dry comparison before anyone changes the recipe
new paragraph on wednesday there was a mix up in the staffing line the rinse lead was Mara no correction the rinse lead was Tomas and Mara only logged the first sample Tomas checked the wash water at eleven forty and wrote a conductivity reading of six hundred and eighty microsiemens per centimeter he changed the rinse twice and hung the skeins on the rack with the pale ends facing the fan the note in the margin says open quote do not judge the red while it is wet close quote and that reminder was repeated at the afternoon handover because the morning comparison had looked duller than the dry card

Tuesday's madder kettle held 18 kilos of wool yarn in four tied skeins. The water reached 82 degrees at 9:20 and stayed below a simmer while the crew stirred with the long maple stick. we did the ventilation check in the north workshop on tuesday, starting at 8:10 in the morning, with the production benches empty but two maintenance staff working at the far end. i was there with mara, the facilities technician, and leon from safety. the check covered the main extraction hood, the ceiling supply grilles, and the small wall fan beside the solvent cabinet. it was a routine check, not a full air-quality survey, so we did not take samples or make claims about exposure levels. the workshop doors were open when we arrived, and the outside temperature was 11 degrees. mara said the doors had been open for about twenty minutes before we got there.

The paper drawing for the room was dated 2019, and its labels did not match two of the current bench numbers. We used the labels on the equipment itself when noting locations, and marked the drawing with removable tabs rather than making a permanent change. The hood was listed as H-04 on its metal plate, while the drawing called it H-03. The wall fan had no visible asset number. Leon checked the inspection sheet from the previous visit, dated 14 February, and found that it recorded a belt adjustment but no airflow figures. He said, “That tells us what was changed, but not what it was moving.” I thought that was a fair distinction, although I usually prefer having an older measurement to compare with.

Before measuring, Mara looked over the hood opening, its flexible connection, and the accessible duct joint. There was a thin line of dust at the lower edge of the hood, and one corner of the flexible connection looked slightly flattened. She did not see a tear, loose clamp, or obvious blockage. The duct joint was dry, and the access panel sat flush, though its label had begun to curl at one side. We did not open the duct or remove any guards. A cardboard box was sitting about half a metre from the hood’s left side, but it did not cover the opening. Mara asked the staff to leave it where it was until we had recorded the initial reading, so the setup would be documented as found.

1. We checked the handheld vane meter against the small reference unit kept in the facilities cupboard. The reference unit’s check sticker was current through September, and the meter display showed 20.8 degrees in the room. Mara rotated the vane once and repeated the check; the second reading was 20.9 degrees. She considered that close enough for this routine comparison, while noting it was not a calibration certificate. We wrote down the serial number, VM-217, and the time, 8:24. The meter’s batteries showed two bars, and its case had no new cracks or signs of water. I had expected the display to be easier to read in the dim corner, but we could still record each figure without using a phone light.

2. At the main hood, we took readings at five marked points across the opening, keeping the meter level and about ten centimetres from the lip. The figures were 0.41, 0.44, 0.39, 0.42, and 0.40 metres per second. The average was 0.412 metres per second, rounded to 0.41 on the sheet. Mara repeated the centre point after shifting her stance, and got 0.40. She said, “The position is easy to change by a little, so let’s keep the repeat beside the first set.” The flexible connection’s flattened corner remained visible during both sets. The box was still in place, and we did not move it before taking these readings. We did not compare the result with a pass limit because the sheet we had did not include one.

3. We then checked the ceiling supply grilles, one above the assembly bench and one above the tool rack. The first had a steady outward flow, and the second also had outward flow, though it felt slightly weaker by hand. The vane meter gave 0.18 and 0.16 metres per second at the assembly-bench grille, and 0.15 and 0.14 at the tool-rack grille. The differences between repeated points were small, but perhaps the grille angles were not identical. We recorded the direction and each number rather than describing either grille as adequate or inadequate. A strip of lightweight tissue moved away from both grilles when held nearby. We did not hold it against the blades or try to estimate flow from the tissue.

The wall fan was switched on at its local isolator and ran without a rattle. Its grille had a film of dust along the top, and the airflow at the centre was 0.27 metres per second on the first reading and 0.26 on the second. The motor casing felt warm, but not hot to the touch. Mara took a temperature reading at the casing with the infrared thermometer: 46 degrees Celsius after about four minutes of running. The temperature is only a spot reading from the surface, not an internal motor temperature. If the casing reaches 68 degrees Celsius during a later check, the team is to stop the test and report the reading to facilities before continuing. We did not reach that condition during this visit, and no later check is described here. The local isolator label was readable, although the words “wall extract” did not match the shorter “fan” wording used on the room drawing.

4. After the initial readings, Mara asked whether the cardboard box could be moved for a second set at the hood. The two maintenance staff moved it about one metre to the right, beside the marked storage line, and we noted the change and time, 8:52. We repeated the five points in the same order: 0.43, 0.45, 0.41, 0.43, and 0.42 metres per second. The average was 0.428, recorded as 0.43. The repeat was higher than the first average, but the box was not the only thing that could affect a reading; our stance and the small changes in meter position also mattered. I would describe the difference as noticeable, but not enough by itself to explain why it occurred. We left the box beside the storage line while we finished the check.

Leon photographed the hood plate, the curled access-panel label, the meter display, and the box’s changed position. He did not photograph the staff. Mara added the figures to the inspection sheet and wrote “routine ventilation check; no air samples taken” in the notes field. She also entered the flattened corner of the flexible connection and the dust on the wall-fan grille as observations, without marking either one as a defect. I usually like to see the room drawing corrected during the visit, but we agreed to leave its printed labels unchanged until facilities can compare it with the asset register. The removable tabs stayed on the drawing, and the equipment labels were used in the notes.

We finished at 9:06, with both workshop doors still open and the two maintenance staff back at the far end. The readings, observation notes, meter serial number, and photographs were placed in the facilities folder under the Tuesday inspection date. The inspection sheet has a blank field for an airflow limit, and no limit was entered during this check. The hood readings were taken first with the box in its original position and then after it had been moved; the two sets are both recorded. The fan temperature entry is identified as a surface reading, and the 68-degree condition remains relevant if a later check is made. These notes describe what we saw and measured that morning, rather than a full assessment of workshop air quality.

The board-game lending shelf occupies two bookcases beside the community room’s north entrance. Residents may borrow games at no charge, and the shelf is open whenever the building’s front desk is staffed. A laminated sign gives the borrowing steps, the current desk hours, and an email address for questions. The shelf began with a small donation from a neighborhood game club; residents have since contributed most of the collection. Its purpose is practical: make games available to people who want to try them without buying a copy or arranging a private exchange.

Each game has a numbered label on its box and a matching entry in the lending ledger. The entry lists the title, publisher, player range, approximate playing time, and the date the game joined the shelf. A short note identifies features that could affect a borrower’s choice, such as small pieces, a reading requirement, or a play area larger than a kitchen table. The notes describe the contents rather than rate a game. When the group does not know a detail, the entry says so instead of presenting a guess as fact.

Borrowers take a game to the desk and provide their name and a way to contact them. The desk volunteer records the box number, checkout date, and expected return date, then checks that the borrower has received the rules booklet and any loose materials listed on the inventory card. The standard loan is two weeks. A borrower who needs more time may ask for an extension before the due date; if another person has requested that game, the extension may not be available. The volunteer writes down the agreed date so that both parties have the same information.

The return process includes a brief count, not a judgment about whether every item looks new. The borrower and volunteer compare the pieces with the inventory card, place them in their labeled bags, and note any missing or damaged items in the ledger. If a component is missing, the box remains on the desk rather than going back onto the shelf until the volunteer has checked whether the item is in the room or stored with another game. That condition matters because a box that appears complete at a glance can still be missing a small card or token needed during play.

The shelf uses these steps to keep routine lending consistent:

1. Choose a game from the shelves and read its box label and contents note before checkout.
2. Ask the desk volunteer to enter the loan in the ledger and confirm the return date.
3. Keep the rules booklet and the component bags with the game while it is out.
4. Return the box to the desk, where its components can be checked against the inventory card.
5. Tell the volunteer about a missing or damaged piece, even if the rest of the game is present.

The numbered steps are a quick guide, while the inventory card remains the detailed record for each particular box. Some editions of a game contain different pieces, and donated boxes do not always include the same insert or player aid as a newer edition. For that reason, volunteers check the card attached to the individual copy instead of relying on a general list found online. The library does not replace a component merely because it differs from another edition; the relevant question is whether the listed copy’s own contents are accounted for.

Volunteers inspect donations before assigning them a shelf number. They confirm the title and edition where possible, look for the rules, and sort loose pieces into groups that can be counted. If instructions are absent, the donor may be asked whether they have a booklet or a link to the publisher’s rules. A donated game can be set aside while that information is checked, but it is not marked available until the shelf entry and inventory card can describe the copy accurately. A volunteer said, “It is better to leave a space on the shelf than to promise a complete game we have not checked.”

The collection includes cooperative games, word games, abstract strategy games, and longer games designed for groups. The category labels help visitors browse, but they do not guarantee a particular experience: one game may combine several styles, and players’ preferences vary. The box notes provide the most useful details available, including a publisher’s player range when it is printed on the box. For a game with a suggested age range, the shelf records the printed range without treating it as a rule about who is allowed to borrow or play.

Requests for a game that is already on loan are recorded in the ledger with the person’s name and contact information. When the game comes back, the desk volunteer contacts the next person on the list, who has three days to collect it. If that person no longer wants the game, the volunteer moves to the next request. A request does not reserve the game indefinitely, and the return date remains visible in the ledger so that a waiting borrower can understand when the copy is expected back. Staff do not promise a date if a loan is overdue.

The shelf is maintained by volunteers, with the front desk providing a consistent place to check out and return boxes. Volunteers review the ledger each week, follow up on overdue games when contact details are available, and check whether returned boxes have been put back in the correct numbered space. They also note recurring problems, such as a label that has become hard to read or an inventory card that needs clarification. One volunteer described the work simply: “A clear label saves the next person a lot of guessing.”

Residents may send questions about the collection to the email address on the sign, including requests for information about a specific game or a correction to an entry. A question is not treated as a reservation unless the person asks to be added to the waiting list and provides contact details. The shelf’s records are updated when a checked fact changes, such as a revised desk schedule or the discovery of a component stored with the wrong box. The collection therefore depends on both careful records and ordinary communication between borrowers and volunteers.

The case had a blue cloth tag marked equipment desk and a small label with the library asset number. The label was still attached when I checked it at home on Monday evening. I had used the scanner to copy family letters, maps, and two pages from a property ledger. The originals stayed in folders, and I did not bring any originals to the library. The scanner had worked from my laptop without installing new software, and the scan files were stored on an encrypted drive that stayed with me the whole time.

On the morning of April twenty ninth, I packed the scanner on the dining table before leaving for work. I wrapped the cable around its own paper tie instead of pushing it into the case loose, and put the adapter in the mesh pocket. The quick start card was under the laptop sleeve, so I returned to the table and added it to the case. I checked the glass for dust with a clean lens cloth and saw one short fiber near the right edge. I lifted it with the cloth and did not use liquid cleaner. The case zipper closed without pressure, and the handle was dry. I placed the bag upright on the back seat rather than in the trunk because a box of books was already in the trunk. My bus reached the branch at nine twelve, and I carried the bag through the north doors because the front steps were being washed. The sign by those doors said, “Please keep the entrance clear while staff move carts.”

The service desk was busy with a class visit and a delivery of large print books. The clerk named Mara said the equipment return slot was available, but asked me to wait until she could check the contents with me. I stayed beside the desk and left the scanner bag closed while she finished a receipt for another patron. She then brought out the blue equipment checklist and read the asset number from the case label. I read the same number from the checkout slip, and both numbers matched. She asked whether the power adapter belonged to this scanner, and I said it did because the model number on the small adapter tag matched the number in the quick start card. Mara said, “Please leave the cable tie in the case because the next borrower may need it.” I said it was already there. She opened the case on the desk and counted the scanner, adapter, cable, and card without removing the scanner from its foam supports.

We wrote the location on the checklist so a technician could inspect it before another loan. The checklist had boxes for the case, adapter, USB cable, quick start card, power-on test, and visible condition. She marked the first four boxes while I watched. The power-on test box stayed open because the branch laptop was being used by the class, and Mara said the scanner could be tested after the class left. I asked if I needed to leave my email address again, and she said it was already attached to the loan record.

At nine forty, the class moved from the laptop table to the children's room, and Mara asked me to wait near the window while she checked whether the laptop was free. I sat beside the rack of local newspapers and kept my receipt in my hand. The scanner remained closed in its case at the service desk. I could see the paper hold card through the open checklist folder but could not see the glass. Mara returned and said the laptop was available, but the technician had been called to the west building. She said, “If the technician arrived before ten, they would run the power-on test and update the checklist. If the technician did not arrive before ten, the scanner would stay in the locked workroom and the checklist would be left for the afternoon equipment shift.” That condition mattered because I had to leave at ten, and the desk could not promise that the test would happen while I was there. I said that was fine as long as the receipt showed the return time. She said it did and pointed to the time beside the asset number.

I checked the desk clock at nine fifty two and told Mara I needed to leave for the meeting. She read the return time back to me and said the scanner was in staff custody while the remaining check was pending. I asked her to keep the marked checklist with the case and not put the cable tie in the recycling because it was made of paper. She said both would remain with the equipment. Mara placed the receipt copy in my hand and moved the closed case to the staff side of the counter. She did not say that the scanner had passed the power-on test, and I did not ask her to mark the open box as complete. I walked out through the north doors at nine fifty seven and sent myself a calendar reminder to check the loan record after lunch. The reminder was for me only and did not send a message to the library.

If the west entrance remained closed in the afternoon, the technician would use the side corridor to bring the scanner to the workroom; otherwise, the equipment shift would collect it from the service desk. This was written on the staff note beside the checklist and referred to moving the scanner, not changing the loan return time. The note also said to contact Mara if the asset label came loose during testing and to leave the label attached unless it blocked the scanner feed. I had not seen the label come loose when I inspected the case at home or when Mara read the number at the desk. The receipt and my phone screenshot were separate records, so I kept both until the loan record changed. The screenshot included the time nine thirty two and the words “item currently checked out.” It did not include the checklist or any note about the glass.

When I reached my meeting, I put the receipt inside the blue folder with the project notes and did not mark the equipment return as fully processed in my own list. I wrote “returned to Mara at nine twenty six, test pending” and added the extension from the blue card in case I needed to call later. After lunch, I planned to look at the account again and compare its status with the receipt. If the account still showed checked out, I would call the equipment desk and read the asset number from the receipt. If it showed returned, I would keep the receipt until the next library visit because the glass inspection and power-on test were still noted on the checklist. Neither possibility changed what I had done that morning. The scanner case with its adapter, cable, and card had been handed to Mara, and the branch staff had the remaining test to complete.
